query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys designed for high-temperature applications, reducing the content of fast-diffusing elements (e.g., Ti) while maintaining adequate Cr and Ta concentrations promotes the formation and retention of a continuous, dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer that acts as an effective diffusion barrier during prolonged oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy similar to the NV1 composition, with a baseline formulation containing standard Ti levels, Cr, Ta, and minor Al.
generation.intervention: Prepare two alloy variants: one with reduced Ti content (modified composition) and one with standard Ti content (baseline). Subject both to isothermal oxidation in air at 1100 °C for up to 200 hours.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C in ambient air with controlled exposure times (e.g., periodic measurements at 48, 100, and 200 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and continuity of a CrTaO4-based oxide scale, with possible dispersion of minor alumina, which serves as a barrier to both outward cation migration and inward oxygen transport.
generation.mechanism: Reducing the content of Ti minimizes the formation of non-protective, porous oxides, which otherwise would disrupt the continuity of the oxide layer. Adequate Cr and Ta, due to their favorable oxidation thermodynamics and lower diffusion rates, selectively oxidize to form a dense CrTaO4 layer. This layer retards further oxidation by limiting diffusion of reactive species (both outwards and inwards).
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy (with reduced Ti) will exhibit significantly lower mass gain (approximately 4 mg/cm² or lower) over 200 hours at 1100 °C and a coherent, continuous CrTaO4-based oxide layer (as confirmed by XRD and microscopic analysis), compared to the baseline alloy which will show higher mass gain and a less protective, heterogeneous oxide scale.
generation.baseline: The baseline alloy with standard Ti content will form discontinuous oxide scales that do not effectively retard oxidation, leading to a higher oxidation rate and mass gain.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for refractory HEAs tested between 1000–1100 °C in air under long-duration isothermal oxidation (up to 200 hours). It assumes that other processing variables (e.g., microstructure) are held constant and that the primary diffusion mechanism is controlled by elemental chemistry.
generation.uncertainty: Variations in microstructural features (e.g., grain size), potential synergistic effects from other alloying elements, and experimental atmosphere deviations may influence the oxide formation mechanism. Additionally, long-term stability beyond 200 hours and under cyclic conditions remains to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with reduced Ti content designed to promote CrTaO4 formation, and a baseline alloy with standard Ti content. Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C for 200 hours under identical atmospheres. Analyze weight gain kinetics, oxide scale composition (via XRD), and microstructure (using SEM/EDS).
measurements: Mass gain per unit area over time via thermogravimetric analysis
Phase identification and continuity of the oxide layer using XRD
Microstructural imaging (SEM/EDS) to assess oxide morphology and barrier integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy with reduced Ti content does not exhibit a statistically significant lower mass gain and does not form a continuous CrTaO4-based oxide layer compared to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis that reduced Ti promotes a protective oxide layer via controlled elemental diffusion would be falsified.

AbstractOxidation behavior of a refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 high-entropy alloy at 600–900 °C was investigated. At 600–700 °C, two-stage oxidation kinetics was found: Nearly parabolic oxidation (n = 0.46–0.48) at the first stage, transitioned to breakaway oxidation (n = 0.75–0.72) at the second stage. At 800 °C, the oxidation kinetics was nearly linear (n = 0.92) throughout the entire duration of testing. At 900 °C, the specimen disintegrated after 50 h of testing. The specific mass gains were estimated to be 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5, and 225.5 mg/cm2 at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 900 °C for 50 h, respectively. Phase compositions and morphology of the oxide scales were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). It was shown that the surface layer at 600 °C consisted of the V2O5, VO2, TiO2, Nb2O5, and TiNb2O7 oxides. Meanwhile, the scale at 900 °C comprised of complex TiNb2O7, AlNbO4, and Nb2Zr6O17 oxides. The oxidation mechanisms operating at different temperatures were discussed and a comparison of oxidation characteristics with the other alloys was conducted.Keywords: high entropy alloys, refractory, oxidation, complex oxides

papers.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.
papers.system: Refractory high-entropy alloys (e.g. NV1 alloy with reduced Ti content)
papers.approach: Thermogravimetric analysis and long-term isothermal oxidation at 1000–1100 °C; microstructural and XRD characterization of the oxide scales
papers.findings: At 1100 °C and testing durations up to 200 hours, the NV1 alloy showed a significantly lower mass gain (≈4 mg/cm²) compared to similar alloys. The alloy formed an external oxide layer primarily composed of CrTaO4 with minor Al2O3 and Cr2O3 dispersions. Reduced Ti content appears to promote the formation of the CrTaO4-based protective layer.
papers.mechanism: A protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier that retards both outward cation migration and inward oxygen transport, thereby governing the oxidation resistance over long exposures.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.
papers.approach: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) in air and in vacuum combined with densitometric analysis and surface imaging
papers.findings: A graded oxide scale develops with an outer Mn‐rich layer and an inner Cr‐rich region. The evolution of oxide phases (e.g., initial Mn oxides transitioning to spinel oxides) was observed with increasing temperature, consistent with the differential diffusion rates of the constituent elements.
papers.mechanism: Oxidation is governed by the differing diffusion rates of the elements (Mn > Cr > Fe > Co > Ni), leading to a stratified oxide structure. While no continuous traditional protective Cr2O3 formed, the gradient in oxide composition may influence barrier properties.

papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of Refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Isothermal oxidation experiments at 600–900 °C; XRD and SEM analysis
papers.findings: Different oxidation kinetics were observed depending on temperature, with nearly parabolic kinetics at lower temperatures transitioning to linear or even breakaway oxidation at higher temperatures. Complex oxides (e.g. TiNb2O7, AlNbO4, Nb2Zr6O17) form, but some oxide phases are porous and non-protective.
papers.mechanism: The formation of complex, multi-phase oxide scales (including porous, rapidly growing V-rich oxides) fails to form a continuous protective barrier, indicating that the balance of oxide phase stability and adhesion is critical.

papers.title: Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata.
papers.approach: Mesoscale modeling using stochastic cellular automata incorporating thermodynamics, kinetics, and microstructural features
papers.findings: Simulations predict that protective oxides such as α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3 can form, with the distribution and scale morphology sensitive to the underlying microstructure and chemistry. In single-crystal simulations, diffusion is limited to bulk processes while phase separation can lead to distinct oxide scales.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between chemical driving forces and diffusion kinetics (including grain-boundary versus lattice diffusion) governs the formation and stability of protective oxide layers.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA with ultrafine-grained microstructures (processed via friction processing)
papers.approach: Stationary friction processing to refine grain structure followed by oxidation testing over 100 h at 850–1050 °C with kinetic and cross-sectional oxide layer analyses
papers.findings: Processed samples exhibit a 12–48% reduction in oxidation kinetics relative to as-cast samples; the refined microstructure appears to favor the formation of continuous, protective oxide scales (chromia and alumina) with reduced effective diffusion coefficients.
papers.mechanism: Increased grain boundary densities in ultrafine-grained alloys adjust effective diffusion paths, promoting the formation of dense, protective oxide layers that slow overall oxidation.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Combination of in situ atom probe tomography (APT), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) to investigate oxide layer speciation
papers.findings: A layered oxide structure forms during oxidation at low temperatures (e.g., 400 °C) with a Ni-rich pre-oxide, followed by Cr2O3 and an outer layer enriched in Fe, Co, and Mn. The study highlights that the oxide speciation is sensitive to both thermodynamic fingerprints (such as cohesive energy, redox potentials) and kinetic factors such as elemental diffusivity.
papers.mechanism: The sequential and spatially distinct oxidation of alloying elements is governed by their combined thermodynamic affinities and kinetic diffusion rates. This interplay leads to the formation of a potentially protective stratified oxide layer under controlled conditions.

papers.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.approach: Varying the Al content in the alloy composition with subsequent high-temperature oxidation testing at 800 °C and microstructural/oxide layer analysis
papers.findings: Alloys with higher Al content transition from parabolic to logarithmic oxidation kinetics, with the formation of a thin, dense, protective Al2O3 layer (~1 μm) and suppression of internal porosity, unlike lower Al content alloys that form thicker (≈25 μm) porous oxide scales.
papers.mechanism: The sufficient availability of Al in the alloy promotes the selective formation of a continuous, adherent alumina layer that acts as an effective barrier to oxidation.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of AlTiNiCuCox High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: AlTiNiCuCo_x HEAs with varying Co content
papers.approach: Preparation of a series of AlTiNiCuCo_x alloys followed by oxidation tests at 800 °C for up to 100 hours; kinetic measurements and oxide scale characterization via SEM/EDS/x-ray diffraction
papers.findings: An increase in Co content correlates with a lower oxidation weight gain and the formation of thinner, denser oxide films. The oxidation kinetics follow a near-linear (n = 1) mode initially, transitioning as the diffusion mechanism becomes dominant.
papers.mechanism: The oxidation behavior is controlled by an interplay between initial interfacial reactions and subsequent ionic diffusion through a developing oxide film, where higher Co promotes more stable oxide scale formation.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: High-temperature oxidation experiments at 700 and 900 °C with mass gain measurements, EDS elemental mapping and kinetic modeling
papers.findings: The alloy exhibited parabolic oxidation kinetics with formation of multi-layer oxides (e.g., outer Mn-rich oxides and inner Cr-rich oxides). The oxidation rate constant increases significantly with temperature, highlighting the influence of cation diffusion and oxygen ingress.
papers.mechanism: A balance between the inward diffusion of oxygen and the outward transport of cations dictates the layered oxide structure, where the formation of stable inner layers (e.g., Cr2O3) is crucial for limiting further oxidation.

established: Protective oxide layers (e.g., CrTaO4, Al2O3, and Cr2O3) improve high-temperature oxidation resistance in HEAs.
Elemental diffusion rates and alloy composition (including elements such as Ti, Al, Cr, Co, Mn) govern which oxide phases form and how they develop.
Microstructural factors such as grain size and phase distribution influence effective diffusion paths and the integrity of the oxide scale.

approaches_tried.approach: Alloy compositional tuning (e.g., reduced Ti, increased Al or Co content)
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced formation of protective oxide phases (CrTaO4 or continuous Al2O3) and reduced mass gain during oxidation; effectiveness is composition- and temperature-dependent.

approaches_tried.approach: Processing to produce ultrafine-grained microstructure (via friction processing)
approaches_tried.outcome: Reduction in effective diffusion coefficients leading to denser, more protective oxide layers and improved oxidation resistance.
Insights into how microstructure and diffusion mechanisms govern oxide scale formation, suggesting that both thermodynamics and microstructural features are crucial.

mechanisms: Protective oxide formation is governed by differential elemental diffusion kinetics that enable a continuous, dense oxide barrier (e.g., CrTaO4, Al2O3) to form.
Thermodynamic preferences (redox potentials, cohesive energies) combined with kinetic factors (diffusion rates, grain boundary effects) dictate oxide speciation and morphology.
Interplay between initial interfacial reaction and later diffusion-controlled growth determines whether the oxide is protective or porous.
disagreements: Some studies emphasize the role of Cr-based (e.g., CrTaO4) oxides as the key protective phase, while others point to alumina (Al2O3) or chromia (Cr2O3) layers as being dominant.
There is debate over the impact of specific alloying elements, as in some systems increased Mn leads to non-protective oxides while in others its rapid diffusion contributes to layered structures.
The relative roles of grain-boundary versus lattice diffusion are not fully agreed upon, especially between single-crystal modeling and polycrystalline experimental observations.
open_questions: What are the precise balances of elemental diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic driving forces that lead to the formation and long-term retention of a protective oxide layer?
How does microstructural heterogeneity (e.g., dendritic versus interdendritic regions) influence the continuity and adhesion of the protective oxide?
What is the impact of extended testing (beyond 100–200 hours) under cyclic conditions on the stability of these protective oxides in high-temperature environments?
How do processing methods and alloy modifications interplay to control the oxidation directionality and diffusion paths at the nanoscale?
opportunities: Combine alloy compositional adjustments (e.g., fine-tuning Ti, Al, and Cr ratios) with processing routes that yield ultrafine-grained structures to maximize protective oxide retention.
Integrate in situ characterization methods (such as HTXRD and APT) with modeling to capture the dynamic evolution of the oxide layer over long durations.
Investigate systematic comparisons between single-crystal and polycrystalline HEAs to decouple the influence of grain-boundary diffusion on oxide scale formation.
Test the effect of controlled variations in the external oxygen partial pressure to refine the understanding of diffusion-controlled versus reaction-controlled oxide growth.

directions.assessment: Varying the alloy chemistry, e.g. by reducing Ti or increasing Cr/Ta contents, directly targets the formation of protective oxides like CrTaO4 or Al2O3. Evidence from NV1 alloy studies shows lower Ti content promotes a continuous CrTaO4-based oxide layer (PMC6513993::web::015::discussion). Physics and thermodynamics support that careful balancing of element affinities and diffusivities can drive the formation of protective scales. The approach is feasible and widely practiced in high-entropy alloy research.

Producing ultrafine-grained microstructures by severe plastic deformation (as in friction processing) affects diffusion paths and enhances oxidation resistance by promoting denser oxide formations (PMC9026100::web::017::oxidation_kinetics). Although indirect, this method tests the influence of grain-boundary diffusion on the oxide scale integrity. It is experimentally accessible but may conflate compositional and microstructural effects.

directions.direction: In Situ High-Temperature Oxidation and Phase Evolution Studies
directions.assessment: Using HTXRD and APT to follow the kinetics and spatial distribution of oxide species in real time directly probes the mechanistic evolution of the oxide scale. This approach can reveal how elemental diffusion kinetics govern oxide speciation. However, it requires sophisticated equipment and interpretation of non-equilibrium data.

directions.direction: Diffusion Kinetics Modeling Coupled with Oxidation Simulation
directions.assessment: Mesoscale simulation (e.g., using stochastic cellular automata) can predict how diffusion coefficients of key species (Cr, Ta, Al) drive oxide scale formation. This approach ties together thermodynamic and kinetic parameters but remains somewhat removed from direct experimentation, so it is best used to complement measurements.

directions.direction: Controlled Oxidation under Varied Oxygen Partial Pressures
directions.assessment: By varying the oxygen partial pressure during isothermal oxidation tests, one can decouple the effects of outward cation diffusion from oxygen ingress. This method directly tests if the formation of a protective oxide layer is governed by balanced diffusion rates. It respects high-temperature constraints but requires careful control of atmosphere.

choice.why: This direction directly targets the elemental balance that governs the formation and retention of a protective oxide layer. Prior evidence (e.g., PMC6513993::web::015::discussion) shows that reducing Ti and adjusting Cr/Ta contents leads to formation of a continuous, protective CrTaO4-based oxide. This approach is strongly supported by established thermodynamics and diffusion kinetics, is experimentally feasible, and permits a controlled comparison between modified and baseline compositions.
